title: Coordinate projections lower generic dimension
statement:
Let $S$ be integral with function field $K$, let
$Y\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^m_S$ be a closed immersion, and let
$X\subset Y$ be open. If $\dim X_K\leq n$, then for every
coordinate $t_r:X\to\mathbf A^1_S$, the fiber over the generic
point of $\mathbf A^1_S$ has dimension at most $n-1$.
An empty fiber is assigned dimension $-\infty$.
The notation refers to scheme conventions.

proof.text: Write $\eta$ for the generic point of $S$ and $\xi$ for that of $\mathbf A^1_S$. Existence and uniqueness of $\eta$ follow from scheme sobriety and integrality. On any nonempty affine open $\operatorname{Spec}R\subset S$, the ring $R$ is a domain and the integral function-field affine-fraction lemma identifies $K=\operatorname{Frac}R$. The affine-space charts $\operatorname{Spec}R[T]$ are integral and overlap nontrivially: two nonempty base charts meet, and their affine-line inverse images meet. Their generic points therefore agree on overlaps, giving the generic point $\xi$ of $\mathbf A^1_S$. Applying the affine-fraction lemma to this integral scheme gives its generic residue field $\operatorname{Frac}(R[T])=K(T)$. Indeed $R[T]$ embeds into $K(T)$, and every rational function over $K$ is a quotient of polynomials over $R$ after multiplying numerator and denominator by the product of their finitely many coefficient denominators. Thus the fiber in question is $F=X_K\times_{\mathbf A^1_K}\operatorname{Spec}K(T)$: the two iterated fiber products represent the same pairs of compatible morphisms, giving their canonical isomorphism by the universal property. Here $T$ acts by the specified coordinate $t_r$, not by an independently chosen function. This reduction does not require $S$ to be Noetherian.

proof.text: The map $X\to\mathbf A^m_S$ is a composite of immersions, hence an immersion. Base change gives an immersion $X_K\to\mathbf A^m_K$, which is locally of finite type. The projection $\mathbf A^m_K\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ is locally of finite type directly from the polynomial chart: its ring is generated by its $m$ coordinates. Composition therefore makes $X_K$ locally of finite type over $K$. For every affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}C\subset X_K$, the affine-pairs lemma gives that $C$ is a finitely generated $K$-algebra. In particular $U$ is of finite type over $K$ (its one affine chart is a finite cover).

On such a $U$, write $t\in C$ for the coordinate. Apply the affine tensor base-change theorem with a singleton family to $\operatorname{Spec}C\to\operatorname{Spec}K[T]$. Its generic fiber is $\operatorname{Spec}D$, where $D=C\otimes_{K[T]}K(T)$. The fiber-ring localization theorem at the zero prime of $K[T]$ identifies $D$ with $W^{-1}C$, where $W=\{h(t):0\ne h\in K[T]\}$. The same generators of $C$ over $K$ generate $D$ over $K(T)$: a fraction $c/h(t)$ is the image of $c$ times the scalar $1/h(T)$. Thus $D$ is a finite type $K(T)$-algebra, even when it is zero. Apply the open-fibre-product lemma with base $\mathbf A^1_K$, open $U\subset X_K$, and the whole second factor $\operatorname{Spec}K(T)$. It identifies $U\times_{\mathbf A^1_K}\operatorname{Spec}K(T)=\operatorname{Spec}D$ with the open subscheme of $F$ given by the inverse image of $U$ under $F\to X_K$. These inverse images cover $F$ because the affine opens $U$ cover $X_K$.

proof.text: Let $Q$ be any prime of $D=W^{-1}C$ and let $p$ be its inverse image in $C$. The localization prime/residue-field theorem says that $p$ is prime, avoids $W$, and identifies $E=\kappa_C(p)$ with $\kappa_D(Q)$ compatibly with $C$ and hence with $K$. Avoiding $W$ means every nonzero $h\in K[T]$ has $h(t)\ne0$ in $E$; so $K[T]\to E$ is injective and extends to $K(T)\to E$. For the irreducible closed subset $V(p)\subset U$, its generic point is $p$, and the closed-subset dimension theorem gives $\operatorname{trdeg}_K E=\dim V(p)\le\dim X_K\le n$. The middle inequality follows directly from chains: a closed chain in $V(p)$ is a closed chain in $U$, and taking closures in $X_K$ preserves strictness because intersecting those closures with the open $U$ recovers the original closed subsets.

source.place: Tag 00E3 (localization primes); Varieties Tags 0A21(6), 0B1C (irreducible closed dimension)

proof.text: Apply the transcendence-degree tower formula to $K\subset K(T)\subset E$. The singleton $\{T\}$ is algebraically independent over $K$, and generates $K(T)$ as a field, so it is a transcendence basis and $\operatorname{trdeg}_K K(T)=1$. Hence $\operatorname{trdeg}_K E=\operatorname{trdeg}_{K(T)}E+1$. The left side is a finite integer at most $n$ by step 4, so $\operatorname{trdeg}_{K(T)}E\le n-1$. Apply the closed-subset dimension theorem again, now to the finite type $K(T)$-scheme $\operatorname{Spec}D$ and $V(Q)$; the residue-field isomorphism in step 4 respects $K(T)$, since it respects $t$ and inverses of every $h(t)$. It follows that $\dim V(Q)\le n-1$. If $n=0$, the equality with a summand $1$ shows that no such prime $Q$ exists, and this affine fiber is empty.

Every finite strict chain of irreducible closed subsets of $\operatorname{Spec}D$ is contained in its largest member $V(Q)$: these members have generic points, and the largest member corresponds to a prime $Q$. Step 5 bounds its dimension, hence bounds the length of the chain by $n-1$. To pass from the affine cover to $F$, take any finite strict chain $Z_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq Z_l$ of irreducible closed subsets of $F$ and choose one affine fiber chart containing the generic point of $Z_0$. That open contains the generic point of every $Z_i$, because opens are stable under generalization. Intersecting with the chart gives nonempty irreducible closed subsets, still strictly nested: their closures in $F$ recover $Z_i$. Therefore $l\le n-1$. Taking the supremum of chain lengths proves $\dim F\le n-1$; if there are no points, use the stipulated dimension $-\infty$. The proof uses prime ideals and topological chains throughout, so makes no reducedness assumption and is unaffected by nilpotents.
